clue.text: An athlete–or a DJ–might, but don't let go the minutes!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an athlete may own a best-ever mark, and a disc jockey may grip a disc
second meaning: keep hold of the written minutes of a meeting

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase works three ways at once: an athlete holds a record time, a DJ holds a vinyl record, and a secretary holds the record of a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Holding a record is owning a sporting best, physically gripping a disc, or keeping the official minutes.

clue.text: A flower has unusual shapes alternatively, a number disappeared.

parts.note: or introduces an alternative
C is the Roman numeral 100
hid means went out of sight

explanation.surface: A flower with odd blooms, and alternatively a number went missing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has unusual shapes' just describes the flower, whose blooms are famously odd; it plays no part in the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The orchid is a large family of flowering plants with strikingly shaped blooms.

clue.text: A choppy pond and a lame thigh combined to make two sound like one on your tongue.

definitions.text: two sound like one on your tongue

indicators.note: the two jumbled words are mixed together into one whole
choppy water is broken up, so the letters of pond are disordered

parts.note: taken as written, the first word to be jumbled

indicators.note: a lame thigh is out of shape, so its letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written, the second word to be jumbled

explanation.surface: A rough pond and an injured leg somehow join to teach a lesson in phonetics.
explanation.definitionFit: A diphthong is a vowel sound gliding between two vowels within one syllable, as in coin.

clue.text: You might do this with an appendix or with an enemy.

definitions.text: You might do this with an appendix
definitions.meaning: first meaning: have it removed in surgery
second meaning: have a frank confrontation with someone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Do this' carries over to the second sense: with an enemy you settle it by an open quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Having an organ out is surgical removal; having it out with someone is a showdown argument.

clue.text: If you ruin game, obviously, you'll be feeling remorse.

parts.note: taken as written
only its opening letter is used

explanation.surface: Spoil a match and you will naturally regret it.
explanation.walkthrough: The ruin is literal and 'game' supplies just its initial; 'obviously' merely links the halves.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue is to regret, so ruing means being sorry or regretful.

clue.text: Gets something for nothing but loses 500 to get pens.

indicators.note: the word for scrounges gives up a piece, here the 500

parts.note: to cadge is to scrounge or beg
D is the Roman numeral 500

explanation.surface: A freeloader drops five hundred and ends up with writing tools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pens' means enclosures for animals, not writing tools.
explanation.definitionFit: Cages and pens are both enclosures in which animals are confined.

clue.text: If this, do you cheer not quite as often or are you more like a rolling stone?

parts.note: to root for a team is American for cheering them on
less frequently, so less

explanation.surface: A question about whether you cheer less these days or simply drift through life.
explanation.walkthrough: A rolling stone gathers no moss: it puts down no roots.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone rootless lacks a settled home, like the proverbial rolling stone that never stays put.

clue.text: One might be all this and no 22, but, nota bene, it's about a large conflict, all rising.

definitions.text: One might be all this and no 22

indicators.note: in a down entry the whole assembly reads upwards, so it is reversed
the two letters for nota bene go around the conflict

parts.note: NB is the abbreviation for nota bene, note well
a war is a large-scale conflict

explanation.surface: Someone all muscle and no intellect, with a note about a great war.
explanation.walkthrough: 22 is BRAIN, so the phrase is 'all brawn and no brain'.
explanation.definitionFit: Brawn is physical strength, the muscle that a person with no brain is all.

clue.text: My angst is disturbed about the very flexible.

indicators.note: disturbed things are knocked out of order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An anxious confession that one's worries concern a supple person.
explanation.definitionFit: A gymnast is an athlete noted for great suppleness and agility.

clue.text: Apply your headgear again, or just tell it all another time?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: put a cap back on

definitions.text: just tell it all another time
definitions.meaning: second meaning: summarise or recount once more

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense splits the word into a prefix meaning again and a cap; the second is the everyday short form of recapitulate.
explanation.definitionFit: To recap is to recapitulate, going over the main points again; literally it is replacing a cap.

clue.text: Proving oral vying is a bad way to create a grand conceit!

indicators.note: a bad way of doing something garbles it, so the letters of oral vying are put in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Showing off your speaking in a verbal contest is an ugly way to build an inflated self-image.
explanation.definitionFit: Vainglory is excessive pride or boastfulness, a grand sort of conceit or vanity.

clue.text: Doing this with Dixie is fiddling around with a slight win, perhaps.

indicators.note: fiddling around with something means tinkering with it, so the letters of slight win are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Playing the song Dixie on the fiddle while celebrating a narrow victory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whistling Dixie' is an American idiom for talking wishful nonsense; Dixie is a song of the US South.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is whistling Dixie, so whistling is what you do with that tune.

clue.text: Obviously, what one does alone to a point–a wise and experienced one.

parts.note: a solo is a performance by one person alone
N, north, is a compass point

explanation.surface: A puzzling remark about doing things alone, followed by praise for a sage.
explanation.walkthrough: Solon was the lawgiver of ancient Athens, one of the Seven Sages; in American usage a solon is a wise statesman.
explanation.definitionFit: Solon was an Athenian statesman famed for wisdom, and his name became a byword for a sage legislator.

clue.text: You and I might be if we argue over these answers, but the symbol of the brand goes to Pa's partner if the chits are bad!

definitions.text: You and I might be if we argue over these answers

parts.note: a logo is the emblem that stands for a brand

indicators.note: chits that are bad are spoilt or messed up, so their letters are jumbled

parts.note: read in the same possessive form: the partner of Pa is Ma, so Pa's becomes Ma's
taken as written, jumbled together with the S of Ma's

explanation.surface: A long, rambling tale about squabbling over crossword answers and a brand symbol passed to Mother.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'answers' are the words of the crossword, and arguing about words is logomachy. The possessive S of Ma's joins the jumbled chits.
explanation.definitionFit: A logomachist is someone who fights about words, which two solvers disputing crossword answers would be.

clue.text: Ancient intellectual, realist, too, possibly, taking nothing away.

indicators.note: possibly signals the letters could be arranged another way
taking, with away, signals removal from the jumbled letters
completes taking away: the zero is removed from the jumble

parts.note: taken as written, as part of the letters to be jumbled
taken as written, joined to realist before jumbling
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A description of a Greek thinker who was also a realist, minus nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: Aristotle was the Greek philosopher of the fourth century BC, a towering ancient thinker.

clue.text: Sounds like a good-looking mode of transportation, but it's an old set of wheels for hire.

definitions.text: an old set of wheels for hire

indicators.note: says the phrase that follows is matched by its pronunciation, not spelling

parts.note: a taxi that is handsome

explanation.surface: An attractive vehicle that turns out to be a vintage rental.
explanation.definitionFit: A hansom cab was a two-wheeled horse-drawn carriage hired like a taxi in the 1800s.

clue.text: Anesthetics or symbols of quantity?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: the figures that express how many

explanation.walkthrough: The first sense rhymes with 'plumbers': things that make you numb.
explanation.definitionFit: Numbers are numerals expressing quantity, and whimsically anything that numbs.

clue.text: Friend of Crick, or Holmes?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: James Watson, the scientist who worked with Francis Crick on DNA
second meaning, sharing 'Friend of': Sherlock Holmes's companion

explanation.walkthrough: 'Friend of' serves both names: James Watson discovered DNA's structure with Crick, and Dr John Watson narrates the Sherlock Holmes stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Two famous doctors share the surname: the DNA pioneer and the detective's sidekick.

clue.text: Is it an instrument of morality or merely less than a grand, as they say?

definitions.text: Is it an instrument of morality
definitions.meaning: first meaning, playful: an upright person is moral, and a piano is an instrument

definitions.text: merely less than a grand, as they say
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the smaller, vertical piano, ranked below a grand piano

explanation.walkthrough: Upright means honest as well as vertical, and 'grand' is a grand piano, not a thousand dollars.
explanation.definitionFit: An upright piano has vertical strings and is the cheaper, smaller relative of the grand piano.

clue.text: Jumps around the queen to become cads and rotters!

indicators.note: the answer goes around the queen to make the longer word, so taking the queen out of that word leaves the answer

parts.note: bounders are dishonourable men, old-fashioned slang for cads
ER, Elizabeth Regina

explanation.surface: Someone leaping about the monarch turns into a bunch of scoundrels.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works in reverse: it describes what the answer becomes once wrapped round the queen, so the scoundrels are the wordplay, not the definition. Bounder is dated British slang for an ungentlemanly man.
explanation.definitionFit: Bounds are leaps or springs forward, so jumps is a straight synonym.

clue.text: This way to the end!

parts.note: the method or route to doing something
a destination phrase that recalls a well-known saying about methods and goals

explanation.walkthrough: Reads like a signpost to the exit, but it echoes the saying 'a means to an end'.
explanation.definitionFit: Means are the methods by which a goal is achieved, as in a means to an end.

clue.text: The support is not out of what the scarecrow lacked!

parts.note: a bra is a supporting undergarment
a batsman who is not out is still in

explanation.surface: A bit of stuffing lore: the scarecrow's prop is all that is left, the rest has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scarecrow in The Wizard of Oz wanted a brain.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Wizard of Oz the Scarecrow journeys to ask the Wizard for a brain, the one thing he lacked.

clue.text: Neither short manuscript meets standards of regularity.

parts.note: nor is the word that pairs with neither
MS is the abbreviation for manuscript

explanation.surface: A brief document that fails to meet the usual rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Norms are the usual standards or patterns regarded as typical.

clue.text: Sounds like a small underground city creature, but it keeps to the beat!

indicators.note: says the phrase that follows is matched by its pronunciation, not spelling

parts.note: a metro is a city's underground railway and a gnome is a small creature

explanation.surface: A little creature living in a city's subway system, yet somehow musical.
explanation.definitionFit: A metronome is a device that ticks at a set tempo so a musician keeps time.

clue.text: Pretty corny!

parts.note: read as 'fairly' or 'rather', not 'attractive'
read literally as made of corn, not as trite or stale

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a sneer at something trite, but 'corny' is taken literally: maize is the American word for corn itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Maize is the cereal plant called corn in America, so it is about as corn-like as anything gets.

clue.text: The remainder before the train wreck shows a bit of control.

parts.note: the rest is what remains

indicators.note: a train wreck smashes the train, so its letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to be scrambled

explanation.surface: What remained before a rail crash shows how a little discipline was kept.
explanation.definitionFit: Restraint is self-control or a measure that holds something in check.

clue.text: Is a little state getting a negative answer in France, or is it just a significant collection?

parts.note: CA is the short postal form of California
non is French for no

explanation.surface: A small US state saying no in French, or perhaps an important body of work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little' means abbreviated, not small: California is a big state.
explanation.definitionFit: A canon is the accepted body of important works, such as an author's or a scripture's.

clue.text: Implying your worst is downhill–or up? This is a person's all!

definitions.text: Implying your worst is downhill–or up? This is a person's all!

parts.words: Implying your worst is downhill–or up
parts.note: playful reading: a best that is level suggests anything worse must slope away
the straight sense: the utmost effort someone can make

explanation.surface: A musing on whether your worst lies below or above your best, ending with everything you have.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking 'level' as flat ground makes your worst a slope; the idiom means maximum effort.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing one's level best is trying as hard as possible, giving every effort available.
